explain.say: Every autumn a forest drops tonnes of leaves, yet the forest floor never fills up. Decomposers eat the dead material and hand its nutrients back to living plants, in a never-ending cycle.

faq.a: Decomposers are living things, mainly fungi and bacteria, that break down dead plants, animals and waste into simple substances. They release nutrients back into the soil and air.

faq.q: What is the difference between decomposers and detritivores?
faq.a: Detritivores, like worms, woodlice and millipedes, eat bits of dead material and break them into smaller pieces. Decomposers, like fungi and bacteria, finish the job by digesting it chemically.
Dead leaves, wood and bodies would pile up, and the nutrients locked inside would never return to the soil. Plants would run short of nutrients, and food chains would collapse.

faq.q: How long does a leaf take to rot?
faq.a: It depends on the leaf and the weather. Soft leaves in warm, damp places can break down in months; tough leaves like oak, or anything in cold, dry places, can take a year or more.
Yes. As they respire, decomposers release the carbon from dead material back into the air as carbon dioxide, which plants then use again in photosynthesis.
asks: Where does the carbon in dead leaves go?

facts: Fungi and bacteria are the main decomposers; worms, woodlice and millipedes are detritivores.
Decomposition returns nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus to the soil.
Decomposition is fastest when it is warm and moist, with plenty of oxygen.
